name: Reduced breathing exercises

lead: Reduced breathing exercises are the core drill of the Buteyko method: practitioners consciously shrink the volume of each breath, keep breathing through the nose, and track progress with a comfortable breath-hold called the control pause. In looksmaxxing circles the drill is bundled with nasal breathing, closed-mouth posture and tongue posture, on the theory that a habit of nasal, calm breathing supports jaw, midface and airway development and reduces mouth-breathing features.

The method was developed in the Soviet Union in the 1950s and has been studied mostly as an asthma aid, where reviews report possible gains in symptoms and quality of life. No published study has tested whether it changes facial structure; the appearance case rests on reasoning from the broader mouth-breathing literature and on practitioner reports.

paras: Practitioners describe short sessions of seated, relaxed nasal breathing in which the breath is made lighter and quieter, often followed by a measured breath-hold to estimate progress. Forum users combine it with mouth taping at night, a closed lip seal by day and tongue posture work. Teachers of the method say the lighter breathing pattern becomes automatic over weeks to months, after which formal sessions can be dropped.

Breath-hold and air-hunger exercises can cause lightheadedness and anxiety in some people, and practitioners are generally advised to stop if distressed. People with asthma, heart conditions or epilepsy are typically told by clinicians to discuss any breathing programme with their doctor, and the method is not a replacement for prescribed asthma treatment.

chain: Supports closed-mouth posture and calmer airway use
Claimed support for jaw and midface posture and a less mouth-breather look
angle.text: Looksmaxxers use the drills to build a nasal, closed-mouth breathing habit that they connect with better facial posture and development. The link to appearance is a practitioner theory drawn from the mouth-breathing literature rather than a measured outcome of the exercises.

lead: Reduced breathing exercises are a set of drills from the Buteyko method in which a person deliberately lowers the volume of air taken in with each breath while breathing through the nose and staying relaxed [1]. Progress is usually tracked with a 'control pause', the length of time a breath can be held comfortably after a normal exhale [1].

In looksmaxxing communities the exercises are treated as one part of a nasal-breathing stack. The reasoning is that habitual mouth breathing is associated with a longer, narrower facial look, and that a settled nasal pattern, a closed lip seal and proper tongue posture together support the face and a calmer appearance. Users also cite better sleep and less puffiness as goals.

Konstantin Buteyko, a Ukrainian physiologist, developed the method in the 1950s; it later spread to Australia, New Zealand, Britain and the United States [1]. Research has concentrated on asthma and, to a small extent, sleep apnoea, with mixed or low-certainty findings; no study has measured effects on facial development or appearance [1].

paras: The Buteyko method rests on three principles: breathing through the nose, including during sleep and exercise; exercises that consciously reduce breathing volume; and relaxation techniques [1]. Reduced breathing exercises are the second element. Proponents say chronic over-breathing lowers blood carbon dioxide and is linked to airway spasm and other problems, and that retraining toward slower, shallower breathing corrects this [1]. Teachers say the techniques become automatic and can later be phased out [1].

Within oral-posture and 'bonehacks' discussions, breath control is grouped with nasal breathing, tongue posture and lip seal. Multi-part guide threads on looksmax.org that cover CO2 breathing for adaptation and humming for nitric oxide treat breathing practice as part of an environmental-factors view of facial structure. Participants describe the drills as a way to make nasal breathing comfortable enough to keep up all day and night.
Related community topics include mouth taping, myofunctional therapy and the nasal nitric oxide theory, each documented in its own entry.

The central theory that over-breathing drives disease has not been confirmed; studies measuring carbon dioxide in practitioners were inconclusive, and many trials have small samples and are hard to blind [1].

A 2015 Australian government review of 17 therapies found no clear evidence of effectiveness for the method; a 2020 Cochrane review of breathing exercises in general found possible improvements in quality of life, hyperventilation symptoms and lung function at moderate to very low certainty; a 2014 British guideline said the method may improve some asthma symptoms and quality of life with little effect on lung function [1].
Human studies of Buteyko breathing have focused on asthma and, in a small number of cases, sleep apnoea [1]. No studies found on facial structure or appearance outcomes.

The Wikipedia summary of the method does not list specific safety concerns [1]. Breath-hold and air-hunger drills commonly produce temporary discomfort such as lightheadedness, and clinicians generally advise people with asthma or cardiovascular conditions to consult a doctor before changing breathing practice.
